There are a lot of OCR models, with more releasing every week. A quick search on HuggingFace for “ocr” shows thousands of models posted. Furthermore, frontier labs are pushing new models nearly every month that also read documents well (albeit at sometimes costly price points). Using these models for document parsing usually requires the same few steps: figuring out prompts (if applicable), handling rate limits, managing deployments and related costs, and benchmarking new models as they come out.

This is something we at LlamaIndex have gotten particularly good at, and today we are launching OpenDocRouter as a way to share that work.

## What is OpenDocRouter?

OpenDocRouter is a platform for document → markdown parsing using the latest open-source and frontier models. Each model runs a versioned recipe consisting of prompts, processing, and settings. Using the API is dead simple:

curl https://www.opendocrouter.ai/v1/parse \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "opendatalab/mineru2.5-pro", "document": { "url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762" }, "layout": true }'

The API accepts PDFs, PNG, JPEG, or URLs to those file formats. The API lets you toggle between synchronous responses (the result is returned directly) and asynchronous responses (a job is created that requires polling). Synchronous responses are supported up to 50 pages. Requests can process inputs that have at most 500 pages or are 50MB.

Every model is benchmarked on ParseBench both in terms of quality and cost. At launch, we selected a set of models covering every corner of our benchmarks:

- Frontier Models: Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 3 Flash, Gemini 3.8 Flash, GPT-5.6 Terra, GPT-6 Luna.

- OSS Models: Infinity-Parser2-Flash, MinerU2.5-Pro, TeleOCR, dots.mocr, PaddleOCR-VL-1.6

## Bounding boxes and layout

Every model makes different guarantees about bounding boxes and layout. Some models output boxes natively, some need prompting, and some can't do it at all.

To close this gap, we built a grounding engine that we can apply to any model. Set layout: True in your request to generate markdown with grounded bounding boxes and layout elements in reading order. This also means all models produce the same layout classes: title, section_header, text, list_item, table, picture, chart, formula, caption, footnote, page_header, page_footer, code, form, key_value.

When new models ship that we can offer, we have processes in place to add them to OpenDocRouter quickly. We run them through ParseBench , and use that to calibrate prompts, costs, and other settings, to give the best user experience we can.

## OpenDocRouter vs. LlamaParse

We view OpenDocRouter as a platform for quickly hosting the latest models, while allowing developers to easily switch and route between existing models, while only paying for exactly what you use. The API itself is easy to use, while providing broad access to models.

LlamaParse is our managed document platform. It ships with hand-tuned parsing tiers, enterprise controls, self-hosted deployments, and other APIs like schema extraction and indexing.

Parsing a page into structured text or Markdown means making a run of judgment calls:

- Is this block of aligned text a table, or just layout?

- Does a header that spans two rows stay two rows, or get flattened into one?

- Is a table that continues onto the next page one table or two?

- Does a flowchart get described, converted to Mermaid, or skipped?

Different parsers make different calls. So two parsers can capture every word on a page and still hand you outputs that mean different things. An agent works only from what the parser hands it, so if the parser groups a header wrong, the agent’s answer is wrong too. But there’s no shared definition of what a correctly parsed page looks like.

The Document Parsing Protocol (DPP) is our proposed definition: an answer key for document parsing, with the reasoning behind each hard call. Today we're publishing working draft 0.1. Its 140 rules cover text, tables, forms, charts, diagrams, and more, and each comes with example pages and the output it expects. It grew out of the rules our annotators followed when labeling pages for ParseBench , our document parsing benchmark.

## The same table comes out three different ways

Here’s a sales page with two header rows. The years run across the top, each spanning its own columns, and the quarters sit underneath. 2023 also has a full-year column.

Three parsers might turn that table into Markdown like this, shown down to the first data row.

Now ask an agent for Q2 2024 systemwide same-shop sales.

- A pushed the quarters into the body, so the 4.1 % column has no year above it. The agent has to guess that it belongs to 2024.

- C dropped the years, so “Q2” matches two columns: 3.8 % and 4.1 %.

- B gets the right number, but only by inventing a label the page never printed: “2024 Q2”. Another parser might write “Q2 2024”, and code written for B would break on it.

DPP counts all three as wrong. It keeps both header rows exactly as the page prints them. Markdown tables can’t show a header that covers several columns, so DPP uses an HTML table. Here’s DPP’s output for the same table:

< table > < tr > < th ></ th > < th colspan = "5" > 2023 </ th > < th colspan = "3" > 2024 </ th > </ tr > < tr > < th >< em > Fiscal year ending December, </ em ></ th > < th > Q1 </ th > < th > Q2 </ th > < th > Q3 </ th > < th > Q4 </ th > < th > FY </ th > < th > Q1 </ th > < th > Q2 </ th > < th > Q3 </ th > </ tr > < tr > < td data-level = "0" >< strong > Systemwide Same Shop Sales </ strong ></ td > < td >< strong > (2.0)% </ strong ></ td > < td >< strong > 3.8 % </ strong ></ td > < td >< strong > 4.0 % </ strong ></ td > < td >< strong > 5.0 % </ strong ></ td > < td >< strong > 2.8 % </ strong ></ td > < td >< strong > 10.0 % </ strong ></ td > < td >< strong > 4.1 % </ strong ></ td > < td >< strong > 2.7 % </ strong ></ td > </ tr > < tr > < td data-level = "1" > Ticket </ td > < td > 6.3 % </ td > < td > 6.4 % </ td > < td > 9.5 % </ td > < td > 5.4 % </ td > < td > 7.2 % </ td > < td > 8.8 % </ td > < td > 6.1 % </ td > < td > 1.9 % </ td > </ tr > <!-- … --> </ table >

The 4.1 % now sits under Q2 inside the 2024 header, just as it does on the page.

## The decisions go beyond tables

Tables are one part of it. Here’s how DPP handles the rest of a page:

- Forms: an empty field becomes [blank] , so you can tell it was left empty, not missed. Checkboxes stay as [x] and [ ] .

- Charts: they become a table of their numbers, with one row per category and one column per series. Printed values are copied exactly.

- Diagrams: they become diagram code, such as Mermaid, when it can hold every label and arrow. If nothing fits, the output describes what’s drawn and keeps every label.

- Hidden and unreadable text: text in the PDF that never shows on the page is left out. Text you can see but can’t read becomes [illegible] .

- Positions: if you ask, each element gets its location on the page, so any value can be checked against the source.

## A shared answer key

Anyone who builds a benchmark, labels data, or reviews parser output has to decide what the correct output for a page is. As the sales table shows, that includes decisions about structure, even when every word and number is right. Today each team makes those decisions privately, so two teams can grade the same output differently. We’re publishing DPP so everyone can work from the same written rules, and argue with them in the open.

DPP also spells out which differences are acceptable. Wrapping table rows in <thead> and <tbody> , for example, preserves the same information as leaving those wrappers out. Both forms conform, as long as a document uses one form throughout. A review should accept either.
